title: Reviewing and reporting progress and lessons
blurb: Describe how progress and lessons are reviewed and reported, and set a reporting frequency and formality that fits the team and the project.
question: A new team has never worked on a project like this. Should the project manager report more or less often than usual, and why?

teach.h: Reviewing progress: as detailed as the plan
teach.body: Formally, progress can be controlled only at the level of detail contained in the plans. In plain English: if the stage plan only says 'build the extension by June', you cannot tell in March whether you are behind. If you need tight control, plan in enough detail (for example, week by week) to compare actuals against. Reviewing progress also covers lessons: the team seeks, records and acts on lessons throughout the project.

teach.h: Plan detail decides what you can control
Reporting: frequency follows the control needed
teach.body: The frequency of reporting should reflect the level of control required, and this is likely to change during the project. A highly experienced team may need less frequent reporting. For an inexperienced team, the project manager or the board may increase the frequency until enough confidence has been gained in the team's capability. Reporting frequency and formality are classic things to tailor.

head: Report
From and to
Frequency set by
teach.caption: In controlling a stage, the project manager reports highlights at the frequency in the communication management approach.
Learn from both mistakes and successes, and share lessons so others can use them.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a new food bank warehouse
teach.body: At Thornbury Community Food Network, project manager Rhys Bennett's volunteer fit-out team has never worked on a project before. He plans stage 2 week by week and asks team manager Priya Shah for weekly checkpoint reports, and the board agrees highlight reports every two weeks. By week eight the team is meeting its targets, so the board relaxes highlight reporting to monthly. Rhys records lessons about volunteer rotas in the lessons log as they arise.

rows.label: Weekly checkpoints for a new team
Virtual highlight reports for a dispersed board
Daily formal reports to an experienced supplier
No interim reports until the stage ends

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) An inexperienced team usually means MORE frequent reporting, not less. (2) Progress cannot be controlled in more detail than the plan holds. (3) Lessons are sought and recorded throughout the project, not only at the end. (4) Changing report frequency or format is tailoring; dropping reporting altogether is not.

items: Progress can only be controlled at the level of detail in the plans.
Lessons are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the project.
Reporting frequency reflects the level of control required and can change.
Inexperienced team: report more often until confidence grows.
Checkpoint frequency is in the work package; highlight intervals are set by the board.

summary: You can now explain why control depends on the detail in the plans, how lessons are captured and passed on, and how to set reporting frequency and formality in proportion to the team's experience and the control the board needs.

A.q: A project board appoints a team that is new to this type of work. What does PRINCE2 suggest about reporting?
options: Report less often to save the team's time
Report at the same frequency as any project
Report more often until confidence is gained
Report by exception until the stage ends
A.why: For an inexperienced team, the project manager or board may increase reporting frequency until enough confidence has been gained (manual 11.2.4).

whyNot.0: Less frequent reporting suits a highly experienced team.
whyNot.1: Frequency should reflect the level of control required, which differs by team.
whyNot.3: Exception reporting alone would leave the board without regular progress information.

A.q: At what level of detail can progress be controlled?
options: The detail in the business case
The detail in the plans
The detail in the daily log
The detail in the risk register
A.why: Progress can be controlled only at the level of detail contained in the plans (manual 11.2.3).

whyNot.0: The business case justifies the project; it does not set the detail for progress control.
whyNot.2: The daily log records informal notes; actuals are compared against plans.
whyNot.3: The risk register records risks, not the planned work used to track progress.

A.q: When are lessons sought and recorded in a PRINCE2 project?
options: At the end of each stage
During closing a project
When an exception occurs
Throughout the project
A.why: The project team actively seeks, records and acts on lessons throughout the life of the project.

whyNot.0: Stage ends are one opportunity, but lessons are captured throughout.
whyNot.1: Lessons are passed on at closure, but they are sought from the start.
whyNot.2: Exceptions can generate lessons, but lessons are not limited to them.

B.q: Who defines the frequency of checkpoint reports, and where?
options: The project board, in the communication approach
The team manager, in the team plan
The business layer, in the mandate
The project manager, in the work package
B.why: Checkpoint reports are produced at the frequency defined in the work package, which the project manager authorizes.

whyNot.0: The board defines highlight report intervals, not checkpoint frequency, which is set in the work package.
whyNot.1: The team manager produces checkpoint reports at the frequency agreed in the work package.
whyNot.2: The business layer sets project tolerances, not checkpoint frequency.

B.q:
Which two statements about reporting progress are correct?
1. Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control required.
2. Reporting frequency is fixed for the whole project.
3. A highly experienced team may need less frequent reporting.
4. Highlight report intervals are set by the team manager.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Frequency reflects the control required (1), and an experienced team may need less frequent reporting (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: frequency is likely to vary during the project.
whyNot.2: Both are false: frequency can change, and the board sets highlight intervals.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the project board defines highlight report intervals.

B.q: A board member asks for a stage plan broken down week by week because the team is inexperienced. Why does this help?
options: Progress can be controlled only to the detail in the plan
A weekly plan removes the need for checkpoint reports
Detailed plans let the board set work package tolerances
A weekly plan replaces the need for stage tolerances
B.why: Control depends on the detail in the plans, so a week-by-week plan lets actuals be compared closely for a team that needs tighter control.

whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports are still needed to report work package status.
whyNot.2: The project manager, not the board, sets work package tolerances.
whyNot.3: Stage tolerances still apply however detailed the plan is.

C.q: Which principle is applied when the board changes highlight reports from fortnightly to monthly as the team gains confidence, and why?
options: Manage by stages, because reporting ends at each stage boundary
Tailor to suit the project, because reporting is fitted to capability
Learn from experience, because each report must include lessons
Focus on products, because reports describe the products built
C.why: Adjusting the frequency and formality of reports to the team's capability and the control needed is tailoring (manual 2.7, 11.2.4).

whyNot.0: Reporting continues within stages; changing its frequency is tailoring, not manage by stages.
whyNot.2: Lessons are reported, but changing report frequency is not what learn from experience means.
whyNot.3: Reports summarize progress; altering their frequency is not focus on products.

C.q: Where are lessons first assessed, and where are they recorded as the project goes on?
options: In initiating a project; in the issue register
In closing a project; in the end project report
In starting up a project; in the lessons log
In managing a stage boundary; in the daily log
C.why: Previous lessons are assessed in starting up a project ('assess previous lessons'), and lessons are recorded in the lessons log throughout.

whyNot.0: Lessons are assessed earlier, in starting up a project; the issue register records formal issues.
whyNot.1: Closing a project passes lessons on; it is not where they are first assessed.
whyNot.3: The daily log holds informal issues and notes; lessons go in the lessons log.

C.q: A project manager reports progress daily to an experienced supplier's board in a formal written report. What is the most likely problem?
options: Reporting is more frequent than the control needed
Formal reports are not allowed for project boards
The board should receive checkpoint reports instead
Daily reporting breaches the stage tolerances
C.why: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control required; an experienced team usually needs less frequent reporting.

whyNot.1: Formal reports are allowed; the issue is proportion, not format.
whyNot.2: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the project manager, not to the board.
whyNot.3: Reporting frequency is not a tolerance, so it cannot breach one.

reteach.title: Learner drivers and experienced drivers
reteach.question: Why does a driving instructor watch a learner more closely than a qualified driver?

blocks.body: An instructor checks a learner's every junction at first, then gives more freedom as skill grows. Nobody checks an experienced driver's every turn. Project reporting works the same way: a new team reports often and against a detailed plan; as confidence grows, reporting can ease. And just as the instructor notes what went well and badly, the project records lessons all the way through.

blocks.h: Reports per month as confidence grows

blocks.text: Less reporting is earned by confidence. Starting a new team on minimal reporting is the wrong way round.

explain.body: Progress can be controlled only at the level of detail in the plans, so plan in the detail you need to control.

test.q: Why might a project manager add weekly milestones to a stage plan?
options: To set the stage tolerances for the board
To remove the need for highlight reports
To allow closer control of progress
To replace the work package descriptions
test.why: Progress can be controlled only at the level of detail in the plans, so more detail allows closer control.

whyNot.0: The board sets stage tolerances; plan detail does not set them.
whyNot.1: Highlight reports are still needed to report stage status to the board.
whyNot.3: Work package descriptions are still needed to authorize work.

explain.body: Reporting frequency reflects the level of control required and is likely to vary during the project.

options: The number of work packages
The size of the project board
The length of the business case
The level of control required
test.why: The frequency of reporting should reflect the level of control required.

whyNot.0: The number of work packages does not set reporting frequency.
whyNot.1: The board's size does not drive how often it needs reports.
whyNot.2: The business case's length has no bearing on reporting frequency.

explain.body: Checkpoint frequency is defined in the work package. Highlight intervals are defined by the project board.

test.q: Who defines the intervals for highlight reports?
options: The project manager
The project board
The team manager
The project support
test.why: Highlight reports summarize stage status at intervals defined by the project board.

whyNot.0: The project manager produces highlight reports at the intervals the board defines.
whyNot.2: The team manager produces checkpoint reports, not highlight reports.
whyNot.3: Project support may help compile reports but does not set their intervals.

explain.body: The team seeks, records and acts on lessons throughout the project, then passes them on so others can benefit.

test.q: Which statement about lessons is correct?
options: They are recorded throughout the project
They are recorded once the project closes
They are recorded by the business layer
They are recorded in the issue register
test.why: Lessons are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the life of the project.

whyNot.1: Closure passes lessons on, but recording happens throughout.
whyNot.2: The project team records lessons in the lessons log, not the business layer.
whyNot.3: Lessons go in the lessons log, not the issue register.
